terms.gloss: trickle out, seep; of a vessel, leak
evidence: Tac. A. 2.23: alveī mānantēs per latera
terms.comment: Of water seeping out, and, as in Tacitus, of the vessel or pipe it seeps from. For water falling drop by drop, stillāre (see “drip”).

terms.gloss: let the rain in (of a roof); rain in
terms.grammar: of the roof or the beams (perpluunt tigna), or impersonal: sīcubi perpluat, wherever it rains in
evidence: Cato Agr. 155: circumīre oportet, sīcubi perpluat
Plaut. Most. 111: venit imber, perlāvit parietēs, perpluont
terms.comment: The word for a leaking roof.

terms.gloss: a crack, a chink (that water gets through)
evidence: Cic. Att. 14.9.1: tabernae … rīmās agunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: For “a leak” as a thing: the crack it comes through. Plēnus rīmārum sum, “I’m full of cracks”, is Terence’s joke for someone who cannot keep a secret.

phrases.latin: Fistula sub lābellō mānat; plumbārium arcessāmus.
phrases.english: The pipe under the sink is leaking; let’s call the plumber.
The roof is leaking; put a bowl under it.

phrases.latin: In vīllā, cum pluet, circumīre oportet, sīcubi perpluat, et signāre carbōne, cum dēsierit pluere, utī tēgula mūtētur.
phrases.english: When it rains, you should go round the farmhouse to see wherever it leaks, and mark the place with charcoal so that the tile can be changed when the rain stops.

phrases.latin: tempestās venit, cōnfringit tēgulās imbricēsque … venit imber, perlāvit parietēs, perpluont
phrases.english: a storm comes and breaks the tiles and gutter-tiles … the rain comes, washes over the walls, the roof leaks

phrases.latin: plēnus rīmārum sum, hāc atque illāc perfluō.
phrases.english: I’m full of cracks: I leak this way and that.

sources: Lewis & Short: mano · Lewis & Short: perpluo · Lewis & Short: rima · Lewis & Short: perfluo
